articles.title: The AI Autocrat
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
Seva Gunitsky is Associate Professor of Political Science at the University of Toronto and George Ignatieff Chair of Peace and Conflict Studies.
Bruce Schneier is a Professor at the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto.
Two weeks after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in March 2022, the Russian TV Channel One editor Marina Ovsyannikova burst onto the set of the evening newscast. She held up a hand-drawn sign behind the anchor’s head that read: “Stop the war. Don’t believe propaganda. They’re lying to you!” She shouted, “No to war!” until she was dragged away.
No one has protested the war on Russian television since then, partly as a result of tighter security and a general climate of fear. But in October 2024, Margarita Simonyan, one of Russia’s chief propagandists, gave another explanation. A growing number of the RT network’s anchors, she explained to an interviewer, are not real. “That face doesn’t exist. We generated the voice and everything else.” They were, she meant, produced by artificial intelligence. In a follow-up interview with the newspaper Vedomosti, she spelled out the logic: “These anchors don’t need a salary or insurance,” she said. “They won’t get arrested, and the police won’t search their homes. It’s all wonderful and terrifying at the same time.”
This is AI’s promise to every autocratic ruler: the ability to maintain control without delegating tasks to unreliable humans. It is an extremely attractive prospect. No matter how powerful, dictators have always needed subordinates—censors, propagandists, security guards, police officers, intelligence analysts, and local bureaucrats—to carry out their orders. But subordinates always pose a potential threat. They could shirk, steal, lie, leak, or conspire against their boss. As a result, one of the oldest dilemmas facing autocrats is how to empower agents to carry out orders without also enabling them to turn against their leader. Autocrats have usually managed the tradeoff by filling key positions with mediocrities whose incapacity is, as the political theorist Hannah Arendt put it, “the best guarantee of their loyalty.” But this inevitably makes it harder for dictatorships to govern and survive crises.
AI appears to offer autocrats two ways to resolve this long-standing dilemma. First, it means they can now easily monitor and discipline their followers in real time. A change in a local official’s spending habits or meeting schedules can be flagged automatically by an AI system, without any need for self-interested informants. Second, AI can eliminate underlings altogether. By automating tasks that once required human discretion, rulers can replace unreliable intermediaries with faithful algorithms that cannot be bribed or manipulated. Officials in autocratic regimes have said as much. AI “can definitely replace half of officials,” Russia’s Digital Development Minister, Maksut Shadaev, told a Moscow data forum in April 2025, adding, “maybe slightly more.”
Yet these promises of a self-running state are illusory, because AI is never truly autonomous. Systems have to be built and maintained by a cadre of engineers and data scientists whose expertise political leaders cannot evaluate. The ruler who turns to AI to reduce a dependence on unreliable humans may end up relying, more blindly than before, on the few AI specialists who keep the system running. And this new digital Praetorian Guard may have the same weaknesses as the old, which makes it a threat to the ruler.
China is in the lead when it comes to developing AI systems that can monitor or replace subordinates. Smart city programs in Beijing, Shanghai, and other urban centers use AI to track performance and centralize oversight of local officials who once operated in comfortable obscurity, subjecting them to an algorithmic performance review. China also developed a “Zero Trust AI system,” which it deployed across roughly 30 counties and cities over the past decade. This system cross-referenced more than 150 government databases to catch embezzlement and nepotism by local officials. It worked a little too well, flagging 8,700 officials before local governments, under pressure from the bureaucrats it was monitoring, began rolling it back. But Beijing has not gotten rid of its new e-government portals, which use automated systems for issuing documents and permits, reducing face-to-face interactions that bred petty corruption or favoritism. The Chinese Communist Party, meanwhile, has plowed ahead with researching what it calls “thought management,” or how to use AI to create microtargeted propaganda. China’s army of Internet commentators, once composed of paid humans, is already being replaced by bots.
Russia has been pursuing the same goals with a similar fervor. Moscow’s citywide facial recognition system, deployed across 200,000 cameras, was used to identify and apprehend protesters during the 2021 antigovernment demonstrations. The central government has started using automated data collection and aggregation to bypass regional officials who could taint the data or use it to promote their own interests. In 2023, Russia’s Internet regulator launched Oculus, an AI system that scans hundreds of thousands of images per day for prohibited content, including political content—orders of magnitude beyond what human censors could process. The Russian security service’s Meliorator tool has been used to create over a thousand profiles of fictitious Americans, primarily on X (formerly Twitter), to spread Kremlin narratives at a fraction of the cost of human troll farms.
Other autocracies are following in Beijing’s and Moscow’s footsteps. In April 2025, the United Arab Emirates created a Regulatory Intelligence Office that uses AI to draft and amend federal laws, work once done by legislative staff. A year later, UAE Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid al-Maktoum announced that autonomous AI agents would take over half of the federal government’s operations within two years and that “the performance of ministers, directors general, and entities will be assessed based on their ability to adopt this transformation.”
These innovations may reduce the number of bureaucrats autocrats need. But they cannot actually create what dictators want most: a self-running state. Even AI-generated television anchors need people to build and maintain them, and censorship systems need people to retrain them as the vocabulary of dissent shifts. Behind every AI model, there is a small group of engineers and data scientists doing essential maintenance, and their work is so technical that rulers cannot understand it.
This dependence thus becomes another form of power. The engineers who maintain an autocrat’s surveillance apparatus, for example, can shape what the ruler sees. They decide what information is important enough to pass along and in what form to present it. They determine which threats get flagged, and they can adjust the algorithms that select what content gets suppressed and who gets arrested. And they can do this without anyone in the palace noticing. Autocrats who turn to AI to escape a dependence on unreliable subordinates have only transferred their vulnerabilities onto a new group of officials.
In fact, this new Praetorian Guard could be more dangerous than previous elites. That is in part thanks to the opacity of AI technology but also because this clique is much smaller. Roman emperors typically had tens of thousands of people serving in the Praetorian Guard; modern autocrats rely on standing armies. But with AI, autocrats will need only a small clique of engineers to build and maintain large-scale AI systems. This might benefit rulers since they will have fewer people to watch, yet it also concentrates points of failure, since a devastating disruption requires only a handful of engineers and makes it easier for members to scheme against the leader. The new guard’s members may also be indispensable. A dictator can replace generals without destroying the army. But running complex machine-learning systems requires such a specialized set of skills that engineers can be difficult to replace without disruptions, giving these actors great leverage.
The importance of tech workers to autocracies has already become apparent. When IT specialists began to flee Russia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, for example, the Kremlin responded not with threats but with inducements, offering tech workers deferments from conscription. It exempted their firms from taxes and subsidized their mortgages. When Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered the mobilization of 300,000 men seven months later, IT workers were granted full-on waivers. This might seem like overkill, given that an AI system needs only a few engineers to run it. But a regime cannot know in advance which engineers it will need, and it cannot train replacements quickly, so it has to hold on to the entire talent pool from which these few are selected.
These measures did not stem the outflow of roughly 100,000 specialists—about a tenth of Russia’s tech workforce—over the course of 2022. But Moscow stuck to bribery, because expertise is extremely difficult to conscript at gunpoint and because conscripted experts might be less likely to do as instructed. Even so, money and privilege cannot guarantee that these elites will stay loyal. Autocrats should recall the lesson of the original Praetorian Guard: for a time, it provided Roman emperors with protection and security. But then the praetorians discovered their own indispensability, and by the second century, they were auctioning off the empire to the highest bidder. This new set of elites can do the same. In June 2023, when the column of Yevgeny Prigozhin’s Wagner paramilitary company moved up the highway toward Moscow, Putin depended on his security services to tell him what was happening. Future rulers in Putin’s position will receive such warnings through machines: intercepted communications sorted by software, camera feeds filtered through recognition systems, regional reports compiled into dashboards. The engineers who run those systems could strike a deal with an upstart challenger and then drag their feet. They could delay the data, let alerts arrive a few hours late, degrade feeds at inconvenient moments, or make a recognition system stop functioning. In that scenario, the ruler would be operating blind. The Praetorian Guard did not need to kill Emperor Nero to replace him. It simply had to abandon him for a rival.
These programmers are unlikely to seize power for themselves, because they are unlikely to carry what coup leaders ultimately require: guns. But there is already precedent for engineers using their power to shape leadership challenges. In 1991, when the Soviet army attempted to seize control from Mikhail Gorbachev, a handful of programmers at the Relcom network kept information flowing abroad and relayed Russian President Boris Yeltsin’s decrees to audiences inside the country and abroad. The plotters could not stop the news of Yeltsin’s defiance from spreading, and the coup collapsed within three days.
AI will not let autocrats dismiss all their enforcers. Someone still has to make arrests and run the prisons, and autocrats can buy loyalty by offering supporters state jobs. But it will let authoritarians downsize, and the number of officials ultimately matters less than how the ruler oversees them. Keeping track of scheming or incompetent subordinates has always been the autocrat’s chief burden. AI could lighten it, letting rulers watch their officials more closely without paying as much active attention.
In the near term, then, AI may greatly benefit autocracies. Despite the many obstacles to deployment, the technology is already bringing autocratic regimes the upsides of cheaper surveillance, smarter censorship, and fewer human subordinates to fear and distrust. But for autocratic rulers, the temptations of artificial intelligence may re-create the same trap they are seeking to escape. The more a regime depends on AI, the more it depends on the people who keep AI running. And those people, like every other praetorian class in history, will quickly discover what their indispensability is worth.
articles.summary: How technology empowers—and imperils—dictators.

articles.title: Why Iran Escalates
articles.full_text:

These, it might seem, are good days for the Islamic Republic of Iran. After years of being diplomatically isolated, economically strangled, and militarily assaulted, the Iranian regime came face-to-face with its nightmare scenario—a full-blown war with Israel and Washington—and survived. The United States began bombing Iran on February 28 with the goal of destroying the country’s nuclear program, its missile program, and even its government, only to fail spectacularly at each objective. In fact, Tehran may now be stronger than it was when the war began. It successfully seized the Strait of Hormuz and shuttered it, sending energy prices skyward. Its armed forces have proved capable of continuing to damage American military bases despite coming under heavy bombardment. U.S. support for the war, always weak, has fallen, and international anger at Washington has spiked. Little wonder, then, that many analysts think Tehran will stay the course over the coming year.
Iranian officials are no doubt proud of how their country has fared against Israel and the United States. They have publicly bragged about their success and even declared victory. But in private conversations, the regime’s elites remain quite nervous. They know that the United States has many tools and tactics it can use to increase the pressure on Iran, and they are concerned that the factors that seem to be holding Washington back—dwindling stockpiles of ammunition, domestic public opinion, and international opposition—could go away, grow manageable, or otherwise become unimportant to American officials.
For the United States, this might seem like good news. If Tehran still fears Washington, perhaps the U.S. government can pressure Iran’s leaders into making concessions. But this misreads the mood in Iran’s capital. The country’s elites have been hardened by the war, which killed their friends and family members. They see February 28, 2026, the same way Israelis see the October 7, 2023, attack by Hamas—as the moment their enemy proved willing to slaughter them, and thus as proof it must be permanently defeated. They never had much faith in American negotiators; now, they have virtually none.
Iran, then, is adopting a strategy toward the United States defined by escalation and continuous offense. That means it will neither stay the course nor compromise with Washington. Instead, it will start doing even more to hurt the economies of the United States’ regional partners and to decimate global energy markets, as well as expand its attacks on U.S. military infrastructure. It could try to assassinate American and Israeli officials. It may even launch ground offensives against its neighbors, including by trying to seize U.S. bases located in Gulf Arab countries.
This approach might fail to make the United States relent. But even if neither side can overpower the other right now and both accept a settlement, peace is unlikely to last. Tehran believes that Washington will regroup and, eventually, start fighting again. The regime is committed to responding forcefully to any American provocation, and perhaps even attacking without one. It does not think it can live with a U.S. presence in the Middle East, so it is willing to go full tilt to get the United States out. Iran’s enduring goal, in other words, will be to make staying in the region so painful that Washington has no choice but to withdraw most of its troops, accept Tehran’s control over the Strait of Hormuz, and acknowledge the Islamic Republic as an enduring power.
When the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, was at a meeting in Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei’s compound. Araghchi had spent the last several months negotiating with the United States over Iran’s nuclear program, but in the preceding weeks, Washington had moved many of its military assets closer to the Persian Gulf and demanded that Iran give up all nuclear enrichment. U.S. President Donald Trump was publicly suggesting that he might try to overthrow the Islamic Republic. Araghchi was in the middle of briefing senior officials on these developments and the growing likelihood of conflict when the bombs started to fall.
Khamenei’s compound was targeted in the initial strikes, which killed many senior officials—including the supreme leader himself. But Araghchi lived. He emerged from the rubble stunned and covered in debris. According to an account he gave to an Iranian podcaster, he ran into the street, stopped a passing car, and asked the driver to take him to the foreign ministry. From there, he tried to reach any military commanders he could and began contacting foreign leaders. Soon, he was joined by other surviving officials.
The Islamic Republic had long anticipated that Khamenei and his deputies might be killed, so it was well prepared to handle the aftermath of the attacks. The government had spent the better part of a year, for instance, decentralizing its political and military bureaucracy so that provincial governors and military commanders could operate without instructions from top leaders. Senior officials had to designate at least two people to succeed them should they not survive. But the experience was nonetheless traumatic for the regime. Iran’s leaders could no longer remain in one place and instead had to spend hours in cars and on motorcycles shuttling between bunkers. They had to contend with the loss of colleagues, friends, and sometimes family. The country’s new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, lost his wife, a sister, and a niece in the attacks—in addition to his father. U.S. intelligence officials say that he himself was injured.
By themselves, these shocks would have been enough to make Iran’s government even more hostile to Israel and Washington than it was before. But the regime’s elites have been further aggravated by U.S. attacks on Iran’s civilian infrastructure, including energy plants and transportation networks. They have concluded that Israel and the United States are not fighting a limited conflict designed to destroy people and institutions that have long ruled the Islamic Republic, but a war aimed at destroying the country itself. They have accordingly adopted a newly forceful posture. Mojtaba promoted hawkish military leaders to take the place of their deceased colleagues and instructed them to prepare for “offensive operations against the enemy.” Mohsen Rezaei, the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps during the Iran-Iraq War, became the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and declared that Iran would target American economic assets and oil companies in addition to military facilities. The country has also started openly attacking Washington’s regional partners. (Before February 28, Tehran wielded military power throughout the Middle East, but mostly via its network of nonstate allies.) Finally, the regime has begun attacking preemptively. In July, for example, it struck bases in Jordan used by the U.S. military, arguing that they were a staging ground for attacks in Iran. In doing so, Tehran killed three American soldiers.
The regime’s fresh approach is designed to do more than deter Washington psychologically. It is also meant to systematically degrade the U.S. military and intelligence infrastructure in the Middle East. In this sense, Iran is developing its own version of Israel’s “mowing the lawn” strategy, in which it carries out repeated, limited attacks intended to weaken an adversary’s capabilities between major rounds of conflict. In doing so, it hopes to make the United States less able to protect its allies and its own forces from future Iranian strikes—and thus less likely to stay in the region.
Iranian leaders are pleased with the results of their methods. They believe that rapid and massive escalation across the region forced Israel and the United States to limit their strikes on Iran’s civilian infrastructure and helped calm the war down.
Yet Iranian elites do not think Tehran has fully prevailed. U.S. and Israeli officials have spent decades predicting that the Islamic Republic is about to fall, and even after its surprisingly strong military performance, they continue to portray it as weak. In September, for example, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the country was “in a death spiral.” To the regime, this perception gap is dangerous. Iranian officials believe that if Washington thinks the government is one sanction, one attack, or one protest away from collapse, it will not stop applying economic and military pressure. Before his death, the elder Khamenei both privately and publicly warned that Washington would not leave Iran alone until U.S. officials could simply not deny its military power. And last August, Mojtaba instructed Iran’s military to achieve what he called “maximum deterrence” against the United States.
In the past, some Iranian leaders thought that they might be able to negotiate a peaceful coexistence with the United States. But now, almost no one in the regime thinks this is the case. Instead, Tehran has concluded that the United States will never be a good-faith partner. Washington’s track record, after all, is defined by betrayal. It pulled out of the 2015 nuclear deal after just three years. When it struck Iran in both June 2025 and February 2026, the two sides were in the middle of talks. And in Tehran’s view, the United States is responsible for the collapse of their most recent peace attempt—the “memorandum of understanding” the two countries signed in June—by trying to open a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Iranian regime also worries that its favorable position will not last forever. With enough time, the global economy could find alternative export routes from those in the Persian Gulf, making the closure of the strait ineffective. Washington, meanwhile, could gain a stronger hand. Iranian leaders think that Trump is constrained for now because he wants Republicans to win the upcoming midterm elections, and expanding the war with Iran has been deeply unpopular. But once that election has passed, the president will not have to worry as much about his approval numbers. Tehran could hold out for a Democrat to win in 2028, but it does not think this outcome will help it much, either. President Joe Biden promised to return to the 2015 nuclear deal while campaigning, only to unsuccessfully try leveraging Trump’s first-term “maximum pressure” sanctions to gain concessions once in office. The next administration might similarly feel that it is locked in conflict with Iran and thus press ahead. In fact, a more moderate president could prove even more dangerous to the Islamic Republic by mending Washington’s international relationships and getting Asian, European, and Middle Eastern partners to help more with its campaign against Iran.
The regime, then, is unlikely to sit tight. Instead, it will start increasing the pressure on Washington now. It can do so through a variety of mechanisms. The government might start, for example, by fully throttling gas and oil exports from the Persian Gulf. Tehran has already cut off much of this trade by closing the Strait of Hormuz, but some Gulf states can still access the Indian Ocean directly or by transiting the Red Sea. To choke off these countries, Iran could directly attack their oil production facilities and ports. It could also coordinate with its Houthi allies in Yemen to shut down the Red Sea by threatening to bomb ships crossing it, as the group did during much of Israel’s war in Gaza. The Houthis have put themselves in a strong position to again shutter that waterway by seizing more territory from Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. In response, Riyadh temporarily shut down the pipeline it uses to transport oil from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea.
Iran could also intensify its attacks on its direct antagonists. That might mean lobbing more drones and missiles at U.S. military bases. It might mean carrying out more cyber-operations against civilian infrastructure in the United States—much as U.S. officials believe Iran did in July, when parts of Minnesota’s water infrastructure temporarily went offline. If attacked again, Iran could more aggressively target the Persian Gulf region’s civilian infrastructure, including by hitting water desalination plants until parts of the region are uninhabitable. Finally, Tehran could try to assassinate American and Israeli officials. For the regime, this would be something of a return to form. Throughout the 1980s, the Islamic Republic and its Lebanese Shiite allies carried out all kinds of targeted killings, taking out Iranian dissidents in Europe and hundreds of U.S. and French soldiers in a spate of bombings. It had mostly moved away from such operations by the late 1990s, as it sought to reduce tensions with other states and acquired missiles and drones as deterrents. But Iranian security analysts are now lamenting the loss of its expertise in targeted assassinations, and Tehran appears determined to revive this capability.
Iran would struggle to assassinate senior U.S. and Israeli officials. The Iranian military does not have access to the kinds of advanced weapons, including F-35 fighter jets, and sophisticated intelligence that enabled Israel and Washington to kill top figures in the Iranian regime. According to U.S. officials, Tehran attempted to hire a hitman to kill Trump in 2024, only for its plot to be immediately foiled by American law enforcement. (Iran has denied these reports.)
But the country does have options. It could, for example, carry out covert operations, or work through its network of regional allies, to kill certain targets. It could also try to kill less prominent personnel. In August, for instance, Iran’s army announced that it would pay anyone who killed or captured a U.S. soldier $30,000.
Iran might decide that it can establish deterrence by simply doing to Israel and the United States what those two countries have already done to it. But if not, Iranian officials won’t hesitate to introduce new tactics. They could, for instance, disrupt global communications. In addition to oil, the Strait of Hormuz carries critical communications infrastructure, including undersea Internet cables that link Europe to South Asia, which Tehran could sever by deploying combat divers, uncrewed underwater vehicles, or surface vessels that drag their anchors across the seabed.
More dramatically, Iran might try to seize nearby land. Israel, Iranian analysts have noted, grabbed territory in the Gaza Strip, Lebanon, and Syria after October 7 and argued that doing so was essential for its security. Iran, they say, should try to establish security zones, too. Tehran will be particularly likely to act if it believes an American ground offensive is forthcoming. After U.S. officials raised the possibility of an invasion of Iran and the occupation of Kharg Island, Iran’s principal oil export terminal, some Iranian analysts and hardline parliament members proposed invading Bahrain and Kuwait and taking over nearby U.S. bases. Tehran could portray such moves not as territorial expansion, but as defensive measures designed to deny its adversaries forward operating positions.
Tehran might apply this same logic farther north. Relations between Azerbaijan and Iran have long been uneasy—some Azerbaijanis view Iran’s Azeri-majority provinces as part of greater Azerbaijan, while some Iranians believe what is now the Republic of Azerbaijan is part of greater Iran—and their ties have grown particularly sour in recent years. Azerbaijan and Israel are close partners, and many Iranian elites have credibly accused Azerbaijan of allowing Israel to use its territory as a staging ground for operations against Iran. Azerbaijan has denied these allegations, but the country is a major oil supplier to Israel, which might be enough to push Tehran to try to seize Nakhi­chevan, an Azerbaijani exclave on the Iranian border. At the very least, Tehran might attack Azerbaijan’s energy infrastructure.
Similarly, Iran could make an incursion into Iraq’s Kurdish region, which it also sees as a staging area for its opponents. In the war’s opening weeks, American officials floated the possibility of arming Kurdish groups and having them mount a ground offensive. If Tehran believes that the United States wants to establish a land corridor from Israel toward Iran—which would necessarily run through Iraq’s Kurdish regions—it might launch a preemptive ground attack. In such a situation, it could call on Iranian-backed Iraqi militias to attack Syria, which would be part of such a corridor, as well. It might also ask those militias to invade Syria if the country’s new leadership facilitates a military campaign against Hezbollah, Iran’s partner in Lebanon. It could even ask the Houthis to enter Saudi territory.
Finally, Tehran could try to do what American and Israeli officials have long feared and worked to avert: build a nuclear bomb. The Iranian government continues to officially insist that it has no intention of constructing nuclear weapons, but many of the country’s elites, including members of parliament, are now arguing that Tehran must acquire them to establish deterrence. It is not yet clear how widespread this view is, and if Iran took steps toward weaponization, it could provoke Israel and the United States to escalate in turn. Nonetheless, if Iran’s leaders conclude that nothing else will stop Washington from continuing to attack, they may decide that going nuclear is the responsible course of action.
Even if Iran does not dash for a bomb, Israel and the United States could respond to its provocations by carrying out more forceful and extensive attacks. Without an extraordinarily costly full-blown ground invasion, however, it is unclear how much more the Israelis and the Americans can achieve. The Iranian regime has proven itself adaptable, and it believes it is caught in an existential battle that it must win. If Israel and Washington carry out even more decapitation strikes, lay waste to critical infrastructure, or put boots on the ground, they will likely end up strengthening the Islamic Republic’s resolve, and the regime will move further up the escalatory ladder. Tehran, after all, will not immediately go all the way to max.
Should Washington realize this, it might respond to new Iranian incitements by trying to reach a cease-fire or otherwise freeze the conflict. But in the long run, this is unlikely to work, either. The Islamic Republic is clear about what it wants—the removal of all U.S. forces from the region—and it is prepared to remain indefinitely on a wartime footing to get it. It could even launch a major offensive without first being hit or threatened, when Washington seems off guard. To do so, Iran and its partners might decide to launch a highly coordinated, simultaneous ground invasion against the United States’ various regional partners and bases and pair it with a massive bombing campaign, including by attacking U.S. naval forces. Its goal would be to quickly overwhelm the American military, forcing it to pull back.
The Iranian regime will need to be careful before launching such an attack, or even before undertaking lesser forms of escalation. Iranian officials are developing ways to circumvent the sanctions and break the blockade, but continued warfare will almost certainly create continued domestic pain. The Islamic Republic is a dictatorship, but authoritarian regimes can pay a price for being too confrontational—particularly when they were facing trouble beforehand. Argentina’s struggling junta, for example, came crashing down after it tried and failed to seize the Falkland Islands from the United Kingdom in 1982.
Iran’s political and military leaders are aware of this, and they have repeatedly emphasized that military decisions must have at least some domestic—and global—backing. In an August interview, Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, declared that his country would proceed according to a logical, rational trajectory in which “the world can come along with us” and Iran’s “own people” would understand “that we are not really seeking war.” But the Islamic Republic’s leadership believes that the Trump administration’s rhetoric and actions have given it lasting support. It claims, for example, that foreign governments are privately telling Iranian officials that they admire the regime’s resistance to U.S. and Israeli pressure. Iranian leaders likewise think they have convinced their constituents that the war is worth the costs. Before February 28, many Iranians were skeptical of the regime’s claim that Washington wanted to “swallow” the whole country, as the elder Khamenei put it, rather than just the government. But after Trump began bombing civilian infrastructure, claimed sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, and declared that Iran’s whole civilization “will die” if the country refused to reopen the waterway, the regime’s declarations seemed much better grounded.
In a sense, Iran has been here before. Right after the Islamic Republic was founded, the country was invaded by Iraq and subject to repeated decapitation attacks by armed opposition groups. In 1981, for instance, a bombing wiped out much of the governing Islamic Republican Party’s leadership. The survivors decided that the regime needed to be more than just organizationally resilient if it wanted to endure. It also needed to retaliate hard against its opponents so that they would learn never to challenge it.
Aside from Mojtaba, Iran’s new leaders are still drawn from its revolutionary-era elite, and they remember this lesson well. They have decided that to stop U.S. and Israeli strikes, they once again must do whatever is necessary to demonstrate their strength, even if that means going on the offensive for years. Tehran is thus more than ready to strike a widening array of targets until the United States gives in.

articles.title: Russia’s Plan to Break Ukraine
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
DMYTRO KULEBA was Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine from 2020 to 2024. He is a Senior Fellow at the Belfer Center at Harvard University.
Since the beginning of July, Russian drones and missiles have been terrorizing Kyiv with exceptional intensity. Air raid sirens blare day and night, warning residents of oncoming fire and sending people running underground. Many of the drones have been shot down, but not all, and the ballistic missiles have largely gotten through, destroying buildings and killing civilians; so far, roughly 100 have died. The bombardments have become so intense that, in recent weeks, Ukrainians have been posting a grim joke on Instagram and TikTok: “Thank God I live in Kyiv, so I do not have to plan for the future.”
Kyiv has now endured almost five years of war, so its residents are used to hardship. But this kind of pessimism is new. For the first half of 2026, observers were celebrating what looked like a turning point in the conflict. After a year of grinding Russian progress, Ukraine learned how to better conduct precise middle- and long-range strikes, allowing it to hit Russian targets far behind the frontlines. As a result, Moscow’s progress came to a halt. The country, which was already losing too many troops, began incurring casualties that seemed unsustainable. Many analysts began to speculate that the Kremlin might soon have no choice but to settle.
But Ukraine’s new capabilities could not deliver victory. And this summer, Russia sharply increased its use of ballistic missiles and deployed fast, long-range, jet-powered drones at newfound scale. It also widened its set of targets. Before, the Russian military concentrated almost all its firepower on cities and towns near the frontlines, particularly in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region. But now it has started mass bombing cities in the interior—particularly Kyiv. It is even reaching places along Ukraine’s western border.
Together, these changes are indicative of Russia’s new theory of victory. Moscow no longer hopes to win by merely capturing cities, or even by degrading Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Instead, it wants to disrupt Ukraine’s whole economy and break the population’s morale by terrorizing urban centers. It aims to make city life so intolerable that residents and businesses flee, and it wants to sever the logistical connections between metropolitan areas. Moscow calculates that this will make Ukrainians increasingly angry at their own government for failing to protect them, weakening the country’s long-admired cohesion and internal resolve.
There is no guarantee that this plan will succeed. Ukraine is large, decentralized, and considerably more capable and resilient than even many of its supporters think. But the country’s economy is in dire straits, and its government is facing budget shortfalls that it needs outside help to fill. Moscow is betting that such help won’t soon arrive. Instead, it thinks that the price Washington and Europe are willing to pay to support Kyiv is limited, whereas the price Russia is prepared to pay to conquer Ukraine is not. Russia’s principal target, then, is not Ukraine’s territory or infrastructure. It is the will of the Ukrainian people and of their partners.
No one in Ukraine has ever been safe from the consequences of Russia’s invasion. People from every city and region have fought and died to protect their state. Stores everywhere suffer from shortages, and the economy has contracted. Still, the invasion has not affected the whole country equally. People living near the frontlines have faced constant bombardments and the imminent threat of occupation, whereas those in the rear can, at times, tune out the conflict.
That is changing now that Russia is targeting places far from the battlefield. In Kyiv, for example, residents used to face a few drone and missile barrages a week—disruptive, but not enough to stop city residents from going about their lives. Now Russia is continuously sending projectiles toward the capital, day and night. On August 27, Kyiv registered a record 13 air raid alerts in a single day. On the night of September 8, a single alert stretched for ten hours, from 7:39 PM until 5:40 AM. Two weeks later, nothing had changed: Kyiv had 11 alerts on September 23 and a nine-hour alert the next morning. A month ago, those of us living in the city would go to sleep expecting a large overnight attack but knowing that it would probably be followed by a normal workday. Today we live with constant sirens and chaos.
So far, Kyiv has borne the brunt of Moscow’s increased bombings. But Russia’s attacks are beginning to hit other relatively protected cities, as well. On the night of July 30, Russia fired more than 20 cruise missiles at Lviv, a city just 45 miles from the Polish border, killing a 35-year-old police officer and injuring 38 people. In mid-September, drones reached the western Ukrainian city of Lutsk, setting a passenger railway carriage on fire. Russia has attacked Ivano-Frankivsk, Ternopil, and Stryi—all cities in Ukraine’s interior. And across the country, Moscow’s forces are destroying warehouses, pharmaceutical distribution centers, and data centers that provide Internet capability. One day, they might take out the facilities that keep Ukraine’s sewage systems running.
The terror from the air has exhausted Ukraine’s society. People are working miracles to keep the economy functioning as they adapt to ever harsher conditions, and they have rightfully earned admiration from across the world. But it is important to understand that Ukrainians are steadfast because they know that capitulating would make life even worse—as Russia’s conduct in the occupied territories attests. Even so, they may not be able to hold out forever. There are no signs, for now, that the country is at its breaking point. But no one can say where that point lies.
To avoid collapse, Ukraine’s government must take several concrete measures immediately. First, its parliament needs to expeditiously pass the legislation required to unlock funds that others have pledged to Kyiv. These laws usually mean higher domestic tariffs and taxes. Ukraine’s lenders, for example, are demanding that it eliminate the tax advantage enjoyed by low-value imports from foreign online marketplaces by applying a value-added tax to parcels, primarily from China, worth less than 150 euros (or roughly $170). Such measures are tough to impose on a population that is rapidly becoming poorer under the pressure of war. They are therefore unpopular with the public, so lawmakers frequently delay them. But the situation is simply too perilous to entertain any more pauses.
The government must also improve public procurement, particularly in the security and defense sector. The problems facing this system, such as prepaid contracts that go undelivered for months, are not systemic, but Ukraine cannot afford any errors. The country must therefore eliminate schemes, such as a kickback scheme at the state nuclear operator exposed in November 2025, that are unrelated to defense spending but capable of triggering major corruption scandals. The country’s National Anticorruption Bureau and Specialized Anticorruption Prosecutor’s Office have made great progress at eliminating graft in recent years, pursuing cases that show officials and the public that no one in Ukraine is immune from anticorruption prosecution. But the government can take further steps to curtail graft.
Still, there is only so much Ukraine can do by itself to shore up its position. No matter how many reforms Kyiv makes, the sad reality is that it does not have enough money to fund itself. The government has estimated that as of September 2026, it will require $52 billion in external financing in 2027 to meet its needs, only $20 billion of which is currently guaranteed.
Traditionally, the United States and Europe have helped Kyiv meet its budgetary needs with grants and loans. But Washington has made it clear that it will no longer provide Kyiv with financial support. The European Union has budgeted roughly $100 billion in assistance for 2026 and 2027, but it is reluctant to earmark more, given that its countries are confronting financial and political pressures. The most obvious solution would be for the EU to provide Ukraine with Russia’s frozen assets, which amount to $300 billion. The bloc’s members generally support giving this money to Kyiv. But most of it is locked in Euroclear, a Belgian securities depository, and Brussels fears that handing over the assets will result in court cases that eventually force it to pay Moscow back. The European Central Bank and Brussels also fear that confiscating Russia’s reserves would damage the euro’s standing and Belgium’s reputation as a financial safe haven. And Washington, for its part, wants the assets to remain frozen so it can use them as leverage with Moscow. But if EU states are unable to meet Ukraine’s financial needs themselves, they will need to ignore U.S. concerns and allay Belgium’s by jointly underwriting the latter’s legal exposure. Even if they decide they can pay more themselves, the choice between taking money from their own pockets or Russia’s should be obvious.
The EU should also overcome its taboo on financing the pay of Ukrainian service members. Although European funds let Kyiv buy all kinds of weapons, the continent has long considered it unacceptable to cover personnel costs. This rule makes no sense from Europe’s perspective: there is no moral distinction between paying for ammunition and paying the people firing it. But it does mean something to Kyiv. Paying Ukrainian soldiers is the government’s most essential and expensive task. (This year, the country is on pace to spend $35 billion on military personnel.) As a result, it is a source of enormous stress for Ukrainian officials and eats up a large share of Ukraine’s tax revenue. If at least some of the cost of paying soldiers were underwritten by external sources, Kyiv would feel more certain about the state of its military budget and thus be willing to channel resources into shoring up its overall economy.
Europe, of course, should also do more to help Ukraine produce weapons. But this aid should be better calibrated. Right now, for example, most of the discussion of supplying Kyiv with arms focuses on providing more missile and drone interceptors. Yet although supplying air defenses is essential, protecting Ukraine’s skies cannot be the only strategy, because of simple arithmetic. The United States’ stockpile of Patriot interceptors is running low, and the country produces, at most, 840 per year, which it must distribute between itself and all its partners. Russia, by contrast, produces more than 1,200 new ballistic and quasi-ballistic missiles per year, which it then supplements with missiles from North Korea.
Eventually, Ukrainians will likely invent air defenses that can be made more quickly and cheaply than those currently in existence—much as they have created cutting-edge attack drones. But until then, Kyiv needs to get ahead of Moscow and stop its ability to wreak aerial havoc. That means striking Russian production facilities, launch systems, and logistics. Western capitals, in turn, could quickly provide Kyiv with more long-range weapons and lift all political and technical restrictions on how they can be used. Such limits do not amount to prudence. They allow Moscow to use Russia’s interior as a sanctuary and reinforce Russian President Vladimir Putin’s belief that he can continue the war without facing additional consequences.
Many Western officials understand very well what Ukraine needs and what they should do. But almost five years into the war, they have started to grumble about the need to keep supporting Kyiv. Some leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump, even oppose increasing pressure on Putin and hope to sweet talk him into making a deal.
But the reality is that diplomacy will not be able to stop the conflict. Even if Kyiv agreed to cede the Donbas territory it still holds, as Russia has demanded, the Kremlin would remain unsatisfied. For years, Putin has been ideologically committed to subjugating all of Ukraine, attacking and reattacking the country in order to control all of it. Now he has effectively locked himself into a state of permanent warfare. The president has reworked Russia’s economy and political system around the conflict, channeling investment into weapons factories and making loud proponents of the war central figures in the country’s government. As a result, ending it would pose greater risk to his regime than continuing and expanding the fighting.
Some Western leaders seem tempted to cut Kyiv off, anyway, believing it to be of little importance to their governments. But such thinking is backward: helping Ukraine to definitively end the war is very much in NATO’s self-interest. Consider, first, the relative economic costs. A recent Norwegian study by the Oslo-based consultancy Corisk and the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs found that a Russian victory would cost Europe roughly $1.3 to 1.8 trillion over four years. The cost of adequately supporting Ukraine over the same four years, by contrast, is roughly $570 to 910 billion.
Russia might also strike NATO territory, including before the current war ends. Putin’s ambitions, after all, go beyond just this one neighbor. For 20 years, Russian propaganda has portrayed Washington and all of Europe as the country’s enemies. The draft treaties he presented to the United States in December 2021, as American officials tried to avert war, demanded that NATO roll back its presence to the alliance’s 1997 borders. And Putin is now engaging in all kinds of provocations against NATO states, including by floating drones over the alliance’s territory. As a result, many senior Western officials are finally warning that a Russian attack on the EU is entirely plausible. Although Russia may not wait until it has achieved its aims in Ukraine to start such an operation, if it does, the resulting conflict would prove particularly devastating. Ukraine’s army is currently the only real counterweight to Russian military power on the continent, and it would then be turned against Europe itself.
Offering help to Ukraine now, by contrast, would help NATO absorb much of the knowledge that has made Kyiv’s forces so effective. Ukrainian defense firms have made major innovations that they are already sharing with their partners and that they could transfer more of. But Ukrainian companies suffer from a shortage of capital and a lack of secure locations where they can expand production. (Only about 30 percent of the production capacity of Ukrainian defense companies, for example, is currently funded.) Europe should thus launch more joint ventures with Ukrainian manufacturers on EU territory, sign additional long-term procurement contracts with Ukrainian manufacturers that can attract private capital, and give Ukrainian companies full access to European defense financing programs such as the EU’s Security Action for Europe initiative. This will both help Kyiv build more weapons and place Ukraine’s extraordinary military engineers inside European factories, giving NATO armies expertise on how to defeat their biggest adversary at a fraction of the amount that they spend currently on weapons. It would thus allow Europe to lift its defense industry to a whole new level.
The Trump administration has made it clear that it will not directly invest any more in Ukraine’s military base. But Kyiv is already using its knowledge to help improve the U.S. armed forces, including by giving the country advice on drone warfare as it fights against Iran. Multiple top American officials, including Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, have declared that Washington has much to learn from Ukraine. It is thus high time for the administration and for Congress to encourage private U.S. investment in Ukraine’s defense sector.
The best way to better integrate Ukraine’s defense innovations into Western militaries would, of course, be to admit Kyiv into Western institutions. When it comes to NATO, such an outcome is unlikely to take place in the near future, given U.S. and German objections. The European Union, by contrast, still says Ukraine will join its ranks—but it has been vague about when or by what process. The body must start providing more clarity on both fronts. Ukrainians do not expect to enter the European Union tomorrow. But they do expect regular evidence that the path toward full membership is steady and irreversible. The country’s people sustain themselves with the hope that they are suffering for the quiet and dignified life already enjoyed by citizens elsewhere in Europe, and a clear path toward joining the EU will strengthen their will.
For years, Western leaders have failed to understand Moscow’s thinking. Now, as NATO officials work through how to support Kyiv for the next six months, Putin has made it clear that he is reorganizing his state for a prolonged confrontation. He intends to break Ukrainian morale by breaking the country’s economy and external support for it. He is meddling in European politics to turn it away from Ukraine. If the United States and Europe want Russia’s president to lose, they must build the will to outlast him.
Ukrainians remain committed to fighting on. Despite a bleak situation, the country has what it takes to survive the winter. But there will be no cease-fire in the spring. It is thus time for Europe and the United States to make sure that Ukrainians have what they need not only to survive but also to return fire. They need to act in concert with Ukraine to prove that Russia’s theory of victory will not be effective—and to turn Kyiv into a city where people can again plan for the future.
articles.summary: What Kyiv needs to survive.

articles.title: The Two Shocks Upending Latin America
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
DAN RESTREPO is a Senior Fellow at the Center for American Progress. He served as Special Assistant to the President and Senior Director for Western Hemisphere Affairs on the National Security Council for President Barack Obama.
RICARDO ZUNIGA is a retired U.S. Foreign Service Officer. He served on the National Security Council as President Barack Obama’s adviser for the Americas from 2012 to 2015 and participated in Obama’s diplomatic opening to Cuba.
They are founding partners at Dinámica Americas, a strategic advisory firm.
Across Latin America and the Caribbean, voters worried about rising crime have elected populists who promise to impose order and security in their countries. Some observers have read this development as a sign of a regional swing to the right, but there is little evidence of a durable shift in that direction. Rather than ideology, what seems to be driving voters is a frustration with traditional politicians’ failure to solve everyday problems. In the latest electoral cycle, voters rebelled against the breakdown of law and order; in the next, they may push back on rising costs and the region’s persistent social and economic inequalities.
Latin American and Caribbean governments, already operating with limited fiscal space, must now grapple with two external shocks: the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz and this year’s El Niño, a warming of sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean that upends normal weather patterns. Both are fueling inflation, disrupting supply chains, and forcing cash-strapped, indebted governments to make hard choices.
For voters across the region, these twin crises have brought the economy back to center stage. Leaders such as Chilean President José Antonio Kast and Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa, who won office on security-focused platforms, have seen their public standing plummet as economic woes deepen. Argentine President Javier Milei, who in 2023 ran an outsider campaign against economic mismanagement, faces an uphill 2027 reelection bid as Argentines struggle with day-to-day economic challenges despite the country’s macroeconomic improvements.
All this sets the stage for more political swings in the coming years, as climate change and geopolitical shifts generate shocks at a pace difficult for any government to contend with. That turbulence could fuel further polarization and reward populists whose promised solutions are unlikely to fix the structural flaws holding back growth.
But chaos is not inevitable. The region has the resources to adapt to a more unstable environment. Its critical minerals, abundant renewable energy, and strong agricultural sector are exactly what the world needs for food security, advanced technology, and the energy transition. To harness those resources, however, the region will have to overcome profound infrastructure deficits, strengthen the rule of law, and accelerate regional integration. Multilateral development banks and outside actors, such as the United States and Europe, can help by bringing in private investment for shared infrastructure, promoting intraregional trade and regulatory harmonization, and creating value chains where economic benefits are broadly shared. The alternative is a region that lurches from crisis to crisis, and from one extreme to another.
Disruptions to energy and fertilizer markets stemming from the prolonged effective closure of the strait have already reshaped Latin American politics. In March, Kast saw his approval rating drop 14 points after he declined to issue consumer subsidies to soften the blow of rising energy prices. In April, Peruvians, upset by the sharpest monthly inflation spike in the country in more than 30 years, showed how economic anxiety can upend politics and open the door to populists. The leftist Roberto Sánchez unexpectedly surged in the first round of presidential elections but ultimately lost narrowly in the runoff to the right-wing candidate, Keiko Fujimori. In Argentina, despite a burgeoning hydrocarbon sector, higher energy costs have renewed inflation concerns and created a headache for Milei, whose disapproval rating spiked to 63 percent in late April, up from 49 percent at the start of the year.
Given the region’s dependence on imported gasoline and diesel, the economic toll of sustained high oil prices is only growing. The governments of the Dominican Republic, Nicaragua, and several small Caribbean countries have subsidized energy costs—a costly proposition as high prices persist. Elsewhere, governments cannot afford such relief, and consumers have been hit hard. The price of maize, a staple across Central America, rose by more than 60 percent in Honduras from 2025 to 2026. In Guatemala, soaring gasoline prices led to public protests.
To be sure, some countries have benefited from the turbulence in the energy sector. Chief among them is Guyana, whose oil revenues have grown more than 50 percent so far this year. Venezuela has also profited, although the long-term viability of its oil and gas sector remains in question in the absence of a meaningful democratic transition. The Trump administration’s deal with Interim President Delcy Rodríguez already faces congressional scrutiny that will only intensify if the U.S. midterm elections shift control of either chamber to the opposition Democrats. In Argentina, expanding shale oil and gas production has turned the country from a net energy importer into an exporter, boosting its dollar export revenues. Brazil’s growing hydrocarbon sector has also made it Latin America’s largest oil producer and one of the world’s top ten, with room for further growth. And Peru and Chile have offset higher energy costs by exporting minerals, including copper and gold, whose prices have climbed to record highs.
Still, if the strait remains closed—and particularly if the United States curtails diesel fuel exports—countries across the region will face higher energy import costs that will weigh on agricultural production and drive inflation.
This year, the consequences of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz will be magnified by what could be one of the most significant El Niños on record. In the coming months, it will likely bring flooding to Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, Paraguay, and Peru; drought to Central America and the Amazon rainforest; and disruptions to key Pacific fisheries. Having drained their budgets responding to the market shocks of the Gulf conflict, many governments will meet these new challenges with empty coffers.
The region is already feeling some of the effects. Peru has endured heavy rains, landslides, and flooding that has affected hundreds of thousands of people, and the resulting economic disruptions are likely to intensify as the year continues. Colombia, hit by a 7.4 magnitude earthquake in August, faces El Niño–driven pressure on its hydroelectric plants and its coffee output, which remains a major source of export income. In both countries, disaster response is straining the finances and capacity of new leaders who campaigned on security but must now contend with economic fragility.
As Central America faces the possibility of severe drought, food insecurity, and high costs for fuel and fertilizer, regional governments will likely have to suspend fuel taxes (and forgo substantial revenues) to head off protests. A decade ago, a strong El Niño hurt farmers in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, fueling a wave of migration to the United States. Now, with far tighter restrictions at the U.S.-Mexican border closing off migration as a relief valve, those countries face the prospect of growing social unrest within their borders. Lower rainfall totals are also reducing water levels in the Panama Canal and slowing shipping, further straining the already disrupted trade in liquefied natural gas.
Given its expanse and varied climates, Brazil faces the broadest exposure. El Niño threatens soy and corn harvests in the south while plunging savannahs and rainforests into drought and sparking wildfires. Hydropower, which supplies most of Brazil’s electricity, will likely come under strain, forcing greater reliance on more expensive gas-fired, diesel-fired, and coal-fired electricity generation in the north and northeast. That shift could require price subsidies for consumers and slow the country’s data-center boom. All of this is unfolding during a polarizing presidential election between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup.
In Argentina, Milei’s economic plan depends on a strong grain harvest to rebuild dollar reserves and sustain his crusade against inflation. After a prolonged drought that curtailed previous harvests, Argentina needs the above-average rainfall El Niño will bring, but too much could damage infrastructure and reduce yields, hitting export income. Lower agricultural revenue would leave the government with less money, and lower domestic food production would drive up consumer prices—both boons to the most extreme Peronist populists running against Milei in 2027.
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and a historic El Niño arrive just as the region was regaining its footing after the COVID-19 pandemic, which hit Latin America and the Caribbean especially hard and caused the region’s sharpest economic contraction in 120 years. That the region avoided another decade of lost growth is a positive sign. But with external shocks now arriving regularly, governments will lack the fiscal and political space needed to address the structural factors limiting growth and development. Without concerted region-wide efforts to seize opportunities in a shifting global economy, chronic underperformance will prevail.
Latin American countries can do little to reopen the Strait of Hormuz or cool the waters of the Pacific. If they are to weather these crises, they will have to band together in ways that have eluded them in the past.
No region in the world trades less with itself than Latin America and the Caribbean. Governments must find the political will to better link their economies in the interest of achieving growth that reaches ordinary citizens. They must also strengthen the rule of law and exercise greater fiscal discipline. The region’s multilateral development banks—the Inter-American Development Bank, CAF-Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, and a panoply of subregional banks—can help on several fronts. They can provide emergency financing and planning support for disaster response. They can also court more private investment.
If governments in the region fail to address inflation, food insecurity, and other economic disruptions, social unrest will follow. Leaders elected on security agendas, such as Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele and Ecuador’s Noboa, will likely intensify their hardline rhetoric and policies. Others, including Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, who recently launched a crackdown on Venezuelan migrants in his country, will be tempted to stoke xenophobia to deflect blame for policy shortcomings. Argentina’s Kirchneristas—supporters of former President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner—and other economic populists will once again gain ground at the ballot box. As populists are wont to do, they will run on promises they cannot fulfill and enact policies that drive up spending and deficits without generating significant and broadly shared growth.
Beyond the region’s own governments, two outside players can help it avoid the worst consequences of these crises: Europe and the United States. The European Union is already positioning itself as a reliable, predictable alternative to both China and the United States. If the bloc’s Court of Justice upholds the long-sought EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement next year, the EU will lock in free trade with Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. Through its “Global Gateway” initiative, the EU is also supporting the region’s economy with more than $50 billion in public and private investments.
The United States under President Donald Trump is taking a different approach: coercion through tariffs and the use of force. Washington may be able to strong-arm a country such as Venezuela for a short-term resource grab, but such an approach risks squandering U.S. influence in the region over the long term. A stable and prosperous Latin America is in the United States’ interest, and so is keeping key supply chains close to home, particularly for critical minerals and advanced technologies. To that end, Washington should encourage governments in the region, multilateral development banks, and the private sector to build resilient supply chains across Latin America and the Caribbean. Together, they can provide Latin American countries with the financing and disaster-response support the region needs to emerge from these crises stronger.
Despite the challenges they face, the region’s governments have an opportunity to help meet some of the world’s most pressing needs and promote shared growth. If they fail, they will open the door to increasingly extreme economic populists who will only make the region’s problems worse. And if the United States and Europe fail to support economic integration, China will deepen its ties throughout the hemisphere by promising quick, visible wins to governments of all ideological stripes—propping them up in the short term but compounding their difficulties in the long run. Quick wins will not fix the structural flaws holding back growth.
articles.summary: Why the region must brace for a new wave of turbulence.

articles.title: The Scramble for the Open Seas
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
MICHAEL ALBERTUS is Professor of Political Science at the University of Chicago and the author of the forthcoming book The Return of Conquest.
Over the last half millennium, societies around the globe competed to divide up the world’s land. Nearly every square inch of soil outside Antarctica is now owned and tucked within national borders. But the oceans have largely been spared that fate. There were times throughout history when countries tried to gate and regulate the seas, but they were too vast to be controlled for long periods. During the Cold War, as technology made it far easier to imagine partitioning the world’s waterways and seabeds, great powers avoided an unrestrained race to grab the oceans. Most governments agreed to deal with them through a patchwork of treaties and multilateral bodies that sought to guarantee freedom of navigation in international waters and assign coastal seabeds to adjacent littoral states.
That order is now collapsing. The Houthis are disrupting shipping in the Bab el Mandeb Strait, the gateway to the Red Sea. Iran and Oman are planning to charge ships fees for using the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for global energy supplies and fertilizers. In July, U.S. President Donald Trump even floated the idea that the United States could impose its own toll on Hormuz, only to later drop the plan.
Other governments, too, are jockeying to claim international waters and marine resources for themselves. Russia is trying to assert control over vast swaths of Arctic waters and seabeds, China is building artificial islands in the South China Sea, the United States has expanded its claims to seabeds beyond its exclusive economic zone, and many countries are laying the groundwork to mine the ocean floor for critical minerals.
The institutions that have kept the oceans free and open are failing, and great powers have, in key areas, stopped abiding by the rules that have held for decades. States are already making moves to control the seas. If governments rush to claim the world’s waters, as they did its land, they will make global commerce more difficult and encourage a new era of seaborne conflict. A world in which the oceans are carved up will invariably be poorer and more dangerous.
Governments around the globe are taking note of the success of the maritime blockades in the Middle East. Just as Iran announced that it intended to introduce a toll in Hormuz, Indonesia’s finance minister suggested that Indonesia might follow suit in the Strait of Malacca, a critical shipping lane in Southeast Asia that carries roughly 29 percent of global maritime oil flows. (He eventually walked back the idea.)
The closures of the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el Mandeb Strait are just the latest in a series of violations of the norms and rules governing oceans. China, for instance, has routinely flouted a binding 2016 ruling under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) that rejected China’s expansive claims in the South China Sea. Beijing contravenes the decision by continuing to build artificial islands on disputed reefs, infringe on the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, and encircle Taiwan. Russia, for its part, is suspected of breaking UNCLOS rules by using ships with concealed identities to cut undersea cables as part of a broader campaign to unsettle European countries.
This aggression is possible in large part because the institutions responsible for managing the oceans are ineffectual. The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, the body that is supposed to mediate maritime disputes, is slow and lacks an enforcement mechanism. The same is true of the Permanent Court of Arbitration, which makes binding rulings on treaty violations. The UN Security Council, which could levy economic penalties or even greenlight military action to protect shipping, is almost always paralyzed by a veto from China, Russia, or the United States. Punishing undersea saboteurs is further complicated by the rules of jurisdiction. Only the country in which the ship is registered has prosecutorial authority, so perpetrating states can protect troublemaking crews by not pursuing cases.
Climate change will spur new disputes over the oceans. Over the next two decades, as Arctic ice melts, the Northern Sea Route that connects Europe and Asia along Russia’s Arctic coast will see dramatic growth in commercial shipping. It is difficult to imagine Moscow allowing free access to that route. Russia already forces foreign vessels to submit to a complicated and suffocating system of permissions and permits to operate within its exclusive economic zone. It also treats corridors, such as the Vilkitsky Strait off the Siberian coast, as domestic waterways subject to Russian jurisdiction rather than international straits that grant the right of passage.
Fights over the oceans are not limited to controlling transit. As China has come to dominate and weaponize the existing global supply of land-based critical minerals, other countries are exploring the possibility of mining deep ocean seabeds. Areas such as the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the North Pacific between Hawaii and Mexico, the central Indian Ocean basin, and the Penrhyn basin in the South Pacific are studded with trillions of stones containing critical minerals. The International Seabed Authority, an UNCLOS body that regulates such activities, has issued dozens of exploration contracts that allow governments to survey and map the ocean floor, gather environmental data, and test extraction technologies. But the body currently forbids commercial mining because its members cannot agree on environmental standards or enforcement and compliance rules.
Nevertheless, the race for underwater critical minerals may soon heat up. The United States is the only great coastal power that has never ratified UNCLOS. Unbound by the seabed authority’s rules and seeking to diminish dependence on China and meet the insatiable demand for minerals to fuel artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies, the Trump administration is fast-tracking permits for deep-sea mining in parts of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone over which the United States already has de facto control. (Although the United States has never ratified UNCLOS, previous U.S. administrations adhered to many of its standards.) U.S. regulators are expected to rule within the next year on a growing number of commercial deep-sea mining applications, potentially clearing the way for extraction to begin soon. The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, which regulates energy and minerals on the U.S. outer continental shelf, is also holding a lease auction in November for two large tracts of seabed off American Samoa that will be opened for exploration and, potentially, mining.
If the United States moves ahead with mining in open ocean areas, countries that have signed on to international laws restricting extraction, including China, India, and Russia, will likely cry foul. Although Beijing and Moscow already disregard other laws of the sea, they will point to the United States’ mining to justify their own.
As with other forms of rules-based order, ocean governance won’t collapse all at once. Great powers still benefit from certain guidelines, such as the regulation of fisheries, even if they stand to gain from disorder in other areas. Rather, the system will likely die a death of a thousand cuts.
Each broken precedent will make the next easier to ignore or justify. Coastal powers will come to believe that the oceans are there for the taking. That lesson will not stay confined to tolling ships or claiming seabeds. States will assert ownership of fishing grounds, tamper with undersea cables, and, potentially, conquer or besiege islands. The erosion of ocean governance could pave the way for China to blockade Taiwan, Russia to strangle Norway’s Svalbard archipelago, or the United States to seize maritime control around Greenland.
The breakdown of the international maritime order could also spur a scramble for Antarctica. During the Cold War, the great powers signed a treaty that froze territorial claims to the continent and designated it a site of scientific exploration and cooperation. But that treaty now looks fragile. China is rapidly expanding its icebreaker fleet and building research stations on Antarctica that U.S. and European observers worry could have dual-use capabilities, which is banned under the treaty. China and Russia have teamed up to delay the establishment of protected marine areas in Antarctic waters so they can expand krill fishing operations. Melting ice and advances in technology could also open up the continent to mining. If a contest for the South Pole breaks out, a host of countries could reassert old territorial claims and race to build satellite tracking stations in Antarctica for intelligence gathering, surveillance, and other military purposes.
In a world with contested oceans, trade and commerce would slow as ships would have to zigzag across the seas and pay mounting fees at points of passage. Goods would become more expensive and supply chains more volatile and prone to disruption. Rogue actors and governments could hold up critical resources or food supplies for their own immediate gain. The oceans would be divvied up as national territories. And in the wrong hands, marine resources and ecosystems, including fisheries, could face grave and lasting damage.
The conquest of the oceans could ultimately unfold like the conquest of land, with the most powerful countries—or those that arrive first—gaining ownership over resources. The number of geopolitical flash points would multiply as governments rushed to grab their share of the oceans and protect their claims through force.
It took centuries of conflict and state building for land borders to become mostly stable. Replaying that in the oceans would be dangerous and unpredictable. Tracts of the oceans would change hands repeatedly as powers rose and fell and as technologies evolved. New winners and losers would arise in the scramble. The countries of the world once chose to govern the oceans together. But the future could see states duking it out to secure their share of the seas. It would be a tragedy of the planet’s biggest commons.
